newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE-Japan commodity funds eye private assets.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Japan commodity funds eye private assets.

text.p: When Japanese think of commodity futures, many still recall the case of an Osaka commodity broker who was stabbed to death in public 12 years ago after fleecing thousands of investors in a fraudulent gold scheme.
But as Japan forges ahead with its "Big Bang" financial reforms, the commodity futures industry is striving to shake off its murky image and lure individual investors.

"Japan's nascent commodity funds have now reached the point where they are targeting the massive pool of individual assets," said Takeshi Yokoyama, general manager at trade house Mitsui & Co Ltd's investment products section.
"Only very gradually are people coming to understand what commodities are. In Japan, commodities have a negative image. They are considered extremely risky," he said.

As some of the big guns among Japan's banks and brokers begin offering commodity funds, and as government restrictions are eased, hopes are rising that the funds can tap Japan's 120 trillion yen ($1.03 trillion) in individual financial assets.

Experts say some wealthy individuals have already bought into commodity funds since the government slashed the minimum trading unit to 10 million yen ($86,200) from 100 million yen ($862,000). A further cut to five million yen ($43,100) is scheduled for October and a complete phase-out is due in the next fiscal year.
Data compiled by leasing firm Orix Corp shows that individual investors accounted for 6.13 percent of commodity fund sales volume in fiscal 1996/97, up from 2.62 percent the previous year.
COMMODITY EXCHANGES OR GAMBLING CASINOS

Japan's commodity funds are also shunning domestic commodity futures exchanges, still burdened with an image of over-regulated markets that are more like gambling casinos than a place for investing, fund sources say.
They note that commissions at Japan's commodity exchanges are high, liquidity is low and there are no commodity trading advisers (CTAs) with the sort of track record required by commodity funds.
As a result, almost all commodity fund money heads for markets abroad, primarily in the United States, Britain and Singapore.
"If you want to improve your performance, you can't invest in Japan," said Ken Nakawaki, senior manager of the business planning and development department at Orix Corp.

Overall accumulated sales of commodity funds in Japan reached 342.9 billion yen ($2.95 billion) in 1996, up ten-fold from 34.3 billion yen ($295 million) in 1990 when they were first launched in Japan, according to the Japan Commodities Fund Association (JCFA).
Yet experts say the Japanese market is still only about one tenth the size of the U.S. market, which had accumulated sales of $25.8 billion in 1996.
They add, however, that the Japanese figures will surge dramatically if the funds succeed in attracting even a fraction of the Japanese investing public's huge pool of financial assets.
Commodity fund operators say investors can reduce risks by diversifying into commodity futures such as oil, metals or farm products that have little correlation with price swings in stocks and bonds.
SEEKING HIGHER RETURNS
Mitsui's Yokoyama also touted the funds' potentially high returns.
"Some 60 percent of (Japan's) individual assets are sleeping in bank and postal saving accounts with minimum interest. Our top performer has doubled its capital since its beginning in 1992," he said.

He added that average returns for Mitsui's yen -denominated commodity funds with guaranteed capital are 6.6 percent, well above the 0.5 percent return on a five-year time deposit at a Japanese bank account.
As the potential client base widens, the range of operators is also set to expand, industry sources say.
"Banks are coming into the business, including Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi and Sakura Bank," said Tsuneo Fukushima, JCFA's manager of planning and research.

The entry of prominent banks such as Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, Japan's largest, has helped improve public perceptions of commodity markets, which in Japan have been dominated by individual speculators.
In the past, the list of brokers on the Tokyo Commodities Exchange (TOCOM) and of commodity fund managers contained only a few names familiar to ordinary Japanese investors.

Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, which launched its first commodity funds last year, has already grabbed a 26 percent market share, the second-largest after Orix's 38 percent and ahead of Mitsui's 12 percent, Orix data showed.
Experts say additional banks and brokers, with their strong retail networks, are also likely to enter the market.

"With branch offices all over Japan, securities houses have outstanding strength in potential sales. They can sell commodity funds as an alternative to trust (mutual) funds," said a commodity trader at one of Japan's leading trading houses. "Banks have direct contact with people wondering what to do with their cash."

As for Japan's domestic futures exchanges, the government is well aware of their shortcomings and is aiming at reforms, including the deregulation of commissions, that would make them a more attractive place for the funds to invest.

"We would like to see domestic commodity markets develop like those in New York and Chicago," said Naoaki Kurumada, a senior official at Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry. ($1=116 yen)
